questions.prompt: A linear program in the plane is infeasible when
options: the level lines of the objective are parallel to an edge
the intersection of the constraint half-planes is empty
two vertices share the same objective value
questions.explanation: Infeasible means there is no point that satisfies every constraint at once, so the painted intersection is empty. Parallel level lines are the pattern of a linear objective and do not decide feasibility. An unbounded set can still contain optimal points, as a half-strip does for a cost that points back toward the strip. A tie between two vertices means more than one minimizer, and the program is feasible.

questions.prompt: Minimize \(x + y\) on the parallelogram with vertices \((1, 2)\), \((5, 1)\), \((6, 4)\), and \((2, 5)\). What is the optimal value?
questions.explanation: The vertex values are \(1 + 2 = 3\), \(5 + 1 = 6\), \(6 + 4 = 10\), and \(2 + 5 = 7\). A linear objective on a polygon attains its minimum at a vertex, so the optimal value is 3, at \((1, 2)\) only. Reporting 10 gives the maximum. Reporting 6 or 7 gives another vertex. Reporting 1 or 2 reports a coordinate.

questions.prompt: On that same parallelogram, \(x + 4y\) equals 9 at both \((1, 2)\) and \((5, 1)\), and equals 22 at the other two vertices. A minimizer of \(x + 4y\) is
options: every point of the edge joining \((1, 2)\) and \((5, 1)\)
questions.explanation: The two vertices of that edge tie for the smallest value, and the level line of a linear objective through both of them contains the whole edge. Every point of the edge is a minimizer, and the optimal value is still the single number 9. Neither endpoint is the only minimizer. The opposite edge has value 22, so the rest of the parallelogram is worse.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order used to classify a planar linear program from a sketch.
questions.explanation: The feasible set is the picture you are allowed to land on, so it is drawn first. Emptiness is checked next, because an empty intersection has no contact point to read. The level line is drawn only after that check, which is what the third step says. The slide comes last: it needs both a nonempty set and a direction. Reading a vertex before drawing the set has nothing to read.

steps: Sketch every constraint half-plane and mark their intersection.
If that intersection is empty, stop and report that the program is infeasible.
Only after the intersection is known to be nonempty, draw one level line and an arrow toward smaller objective values.
Move the line in the arrow's direction: an endless move means unbounded, and the last contact otherwise gives the optimal value.

questions.prompt: On the parallelogram with vertices \((1, 2)\), \((5, 1)\), \((6, 4)\), and \((2, 5)\), which statements about \(x + 4y\) hold?
options: Every point of the edge from \((1, 2)\) to \((5, 1)\) is a minimizer.
questions.explanation:
The vertex values are 9, 9, 22, and 22. The minimum is 9 and it is attained along the whole edge where the level line lies. The maximum is 22, attained along the opposite edge. The polygon is bounded, so the program is not an unbounded ray.
• \((6, 4)\) has value 22, which is the maximum, not the minimum.

questions.prompt: Minimize \(x - 2y\) on the parallelogram with vertices \((1, 2)\), \((5, 1)\), \((6, 4)\), and \((2, 5)\). What is the optimal value?
questions.explanation: The vertex values are \(1 - 4 = -3\), \(5 - 2 = 3\), \(6 - 8 = -2\), and \(2 - 10 = -8\). The smallest is \(-8\), at \((2, 5)\). Reporting 3 gives the maximum. Reporting \(-3\) or \(-2\) gives a different vertex. Reporting 5 or 2 reports a coordinate of the minimizer rather than the objective.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: A note claims that \((5, 1)\) minimizes \(x + y\) on the parallelogram with vertices \((1, 2)\), \((5, 1)\), \((6, 4)\), and \((2, 5)\). Exactly one step is false.
questions.explanation: The levels of a linear function are parallel lines, and a linear function on a polygon attains its minimum at a vertex. A tie along an edge really does fill that edge with minimizers. The comparison is the false step. The values are 3 at \((1, 2)\), 6 at \((5, 1)\), 10 at \((6, 4)\), and 7 at \((2, 5)\). The smallest is 3, so \((5, 1)\) is not a minimizer.

questions.figure_alt: A segment joining two marked points on the axes.
steps: The level lines of \(x + y\) are the lines \(x + y = c\).
A linear objective on a polygon attains its minimum at a vertex.
Among the four vertices, \((5, 1)\) gives the smallest value of \(x + y\).
If two adjacent vertices tie, every point of the edge between them is a minimizer.
reasons: The level lines of \(x + y\) are circles.
A linear objective on a polygon need not attain its minimum at a vertex.

questions.prompt: Maximize \(x + 4y\) on the parallelogram with vertices \((1, 2)\), \((5, 1)\), \((6, 4)\), and \((2, 5)\). What is the optimal value?
questions.explanation: The vertex values are 9, 9, 22, and 22. The largest is 22, attained at both \((6, 4)\) and \((2, 5)\), so the maximizer is not unique and the optimal value still is. Reporting 9 gives the minimum. Reporting 6 or 4 or 5 reports a coordinate.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping upward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: The level lines of \(p x + q y\), with \(q \ne 0\), have slope
questions.explanation: A level is \(p x + q y = c\), so \(y = -(p/q) x + c/q\). The slope is \(-p/q\). The gradient \((p, q)\) is perpendicular to those lines and points toward larger values, which is how you know which way to slide. Using \(p/q\) without the minus slopes the line the wrong way. Using \(-q/p\) swaps the two coefficients.

questions.prompt: Minimize \(x + y\) subject to \(x \ge 1\) and \(y \ge 0\). Which description is right?
options: The feasible set is a polygon with four vertices.
The feasible set is unbounded, and the optimal value is 1.
The feasible set is unbounded, and the objective is unbounded below.
questions.explanation: The constraints leave an unbounded quarter-plane, cut off only by \(x \ge 1\). Along that ray the objective \(x + y\) is at least 1, and the value 1 is attained at \((1, 0)\). The set being unbounded does not make the objective unbounded. The set is nonempty, so the program is feasible. It is not a polygon with a finite vertex list.

questions.prompt: Minimize \(2x + y\) on the parallelogram with vertices \((1, 2)\), \((5, 1)\), \((6, 4)\), and \((2, 5)\). What is the optimal value?
questions.explanation: The vertex values are \(2 + 2 = 4\), \(10 + 1 = 11\), \(12 + 4 = 16\), and \(4 + 5 = 9\). The smallest is 4, at \((1, 2)\). Reporting 16 gives the maximum. Reporting 11 or 9 gives another vertex. Reporting 2 gives a coordinate.

questions.prompt: The unique minimizer of \(x + y\) on the parallelogram with vertices \((1, 2)\), \((5, 1)\), \((6, 4)\), and \((2, 5)\) is
questions.explanation: The vertex values are 3, 6, 10, and 7. The unique minimum is 3, at \((1, 2)\). The point \((6, 4)\) is the unique maximizer, with value 10. The other two vertices sit strictly between. The center of the parallelogram is a convex combination of vertices and cannot beat the best vertex for a linear objective.
